hypotheses.name: Semicolon-as-antithesis
hypotheses.claim: AI-drafted passages fuse a claim to its own restatement or reversal with a semicolon ("these costs do not disappear; they land on grocery bills"; "it would deliver bureaucratic theatre; it is a showpiece of announcements"); genuine Hansard barely uses the mark at all. Measured: 45% of the 31 seeds contain at least one semicolon (0.61 per segment) vs 8% of the 12 human exemplars (0.17 per segment) — the single cleanest surface split I found.
hypotheses.how: Delete every semicolon. Replace it with a full stop and let the second clause stand alone, or with a plain coordinator ("and", "because", "so"). Never use it to bolt a punchier paraphrase onto the clause before it. Cap the whole passage at zero semicolons; one is already anomalous for a 300-word speech.

hypotheses.name: No closing aphorism
hypotheses.claim: AI-drafted passages land their last sentence as a portable aphorism, almost always built on a negation-contrast: "not through force but through freedom", "duplication dressed up as innovation", "We must build, but build right", "moving forward, not backward", "not free for the taking", "not reform, but reorganization". Roughly 12 of 31 seeds close this way. Human passages stop mid-argument, on a new concrete particular ("...granted an unescorted, 72-hour release in Oshawa"), a procedural ask ("...studied as soon as possible at the justice committee"), or a reservation ("...compel evidence without judicial authorization") — 1 or 2 of 12.
hypotheses.how: Write the ending last and test it: if the final sentence contains "not X but Y", "That is how/what/why…", or could be tweeted without the paragraph, cut it. Replace it with the next unglamorous item in the argument — a date, a figure, a named body, an objection you have not resolved. Human segments are also longer at the end than the AI ones (final sentence 24.9 words vs 21.5), so anticlimax means one more clause, not a shorter one.

hypotheses.name: Full official names, glossed
hypotheses.claim: Human speakers write institutions out at their full bureaucratic length and then gloss the acronym — "the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, or CPTPP", "the Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions", "the Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs", "the Durham Regional Police Association". AI drafts use short generic labels ("the government", "the agency", "police leaders", "bureaucrats"). Measured: 4+-word capitalised name-runs appear in 0.42 per human segment vs 0.10 per seed; acronym glosses 0.17 vs 0.00; multi-word proper-noun density 1.15% vs 0.89% of tokens.
hypotheses.how: For every organisation, court, committee, report, or programme mentioned, spell the registered name in full on first use, add ", or ABC," and use the acronym after. Include at least one name of four or more capitalised words. Where the draft says "the government" or "the agency", substitute the department that actually holds the file.

hypotheses.name: Procedural coordinates up front
hypotheses.claim: Human segments are anchored to the mechanics of the sitting — stage of the bill, whose behalf, what committee, splitting time, what happened at second reading, an interruption from the floor ("An hon. member: No. Carlos Leitão: No? Okay, democracy in action, I see."). Measured: 1.67 procedural markers per human segment vs 0.52 per seed, and the opening sentence carries a bill number, stage, or Speaker address in 50% of human segments vs 16% of seeds. AI drafts open on theme instead ("When it comes to housing, bureaucrats count starts.").
hypotheses.how: In the first two sentences, state the exact procedural position: "I rise to speak on Bill C-25, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act, at the third reading stage"; "I rise on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of X". Then, somewhere in the body, reference the process ahead or behind: what the committee heard, clause-by-clause, when it was tabled, what you said at second reading. Two of these per 300 words.

hypotheses.name: Hand the argument to a named outsider
hypotheses.claim: Human passages surrender the microphone to a quoted third party at length and then gloss the quote flatly — Kirkland runs 90 words of Andrew Tummonds of the Durham Regional Police Association verbatim (typos and inconsistent capitalisation intact) and follows with "Those are not partisan words."; MacKinnon block-quotes the foreign-interference inquiry. AI drafts paraphrase everything into one uniform voice ("The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police has endorsed Bill C-14, stating that it reflects their own recommendations"). Measured: quoted material in 0.17 of human segments vs 0.06 of seeds.
hypotheses.how: Insert one verbatim quotation of 40+ words attributed to a named individual with title and organisation and an occasion ("said it clearly after Bill C-242 was defeated"). Do not clean up the source's punctuation or register. Follow it with a single flat sentence of gloss — not an amplification, not a rhetorical question.

hypotheses.name: Repetition without a payoff line
hypotheses.claim: Both sides repeat, but differently. Human repetition is a clause template repeated three or four times with the same tail and no escalation — MacKinnon's "Their ability to … would remain intact." three times, then "Ministers would continue to testify… Government officials would continue to testify…"; Champagne's four flat "We are …" sentences. AI repetition is anaphoric, escalating, and cashes out in a reversal — Kronis: "They count units. They count dollars. They count funds, programs, agencies and promises, but in Nanaimo—Ladysmith, we count something different." Humans also repeat their most-used content word more (6.7 vs 5.5 occurrences) at lower type-token ratio (0.44 vs 0.47).
hypotheses.how: Build the series on a repeated ending, not a repeated opening. Keep all members the same length and register, use three or four, and then simply stop — no member that inverts the pattern, no "but we", no summarising line after it. Repeat the key noun literally each time instead of reaching for a synonym.

hypotheses.name: Fewer numbers, hedged and sourced
hypotheses.claim: AI drafts deliver numbers as a pre-computed escalating series with the inference done for the reader: "$1.82 a litre, up from $1.32 a year ago and just $1.52 six short weeks ago. That is a 38% spike"; "roughly $92 … more than $127 … Next week, it might be more." Human speakers give fewer figures, attached to the institution that publishes them, hedged, and leave the arithmetic alone: "the 10-year yield on a Canadian government bond is now, I believe, about 3.5%", "long-term gains for Canada in excess of $4.2 billion", "rating second for trade and first for foreign direct investment as shares of GDP". Measured: hedged numerals 0.39 per seed vs 0.17 per human even though raw numeral counts are the same (2.8 vs 2.9) — i.e. the AI hedges are decorative ("more than", "over") while the human ones are epistemic ("I believe", "about").
hypotheses.how: Keep at most two figures per paragraph. Attach each to the body that publishes it (CAA, Statistics Canada, the estimates). Mark one with genuine uncertainty — "about", "I believe", "roughly" placed next to the speaker, not the noun. Delete any sentence whose only job is to convert the figures into a percentage change or a total.

hypotheses.name: Kill the 'It is' definition
hypotheses.claim: AI drafts define abstractions with existential clefts — "It is a privilege, a responsibility and a bond to this country", "It is the distance between a young person with a diploma and…", "It is duplication dressed up as innovation", "It is not a solution; it is exactly the problem" — averaging 0.68 "It is / It would be / It was" sentence-openers per seed vs 0.17 per human exemplar, and preferring abstract nouns as grammatical subjects. Human sentences put institutions and people in subject position and give them dated, documented verbs ("The Chief Electoral Officer, in recent years, called disinformation … the 'most important' threat"; "The committee heard testimony from 27 witnesses").
hypotheses.how: Rewrite every sentence starting "It is", "This is", "That is" so the grammatical subject is a named actor — a department, a committee, a member, a company, a police service — performing an act you can attach a date or a document to. Allow at most one such cleft per 300 words.

hypotheses.name: Speaker-management asides and one ungainly sentence
hypotheses.claim: Human passages contain metadiscursive asides that manage the room and the clock — "if I may—", "Allow me to provide a few examples of this", "I will now go back to the practical effects on committees", "I would observe, however, that I have some concerns", "I see that my colleagues are smiling. I understand why", "I want to be very clear about something", "I cannot fathom how" — 0.83 per human segment vs 0.19 per seed. These asides also produce the passage's one over-long, unbalanced sentence: humans' longest sentence averages 48 words with a 45+-word sentence in 42% of segments, against 40 words and 29% for the seeds.
hypotheses.how: Insert two first-person asides that do nothing for the argument: one announcing a structural move ("Allow me to…", "I will now turn back to…"), one registering a personal reaction or reservation ("I would observe, however, that…", "I must say I cannot fathom…"). Let the second one run: chain a relative clause onto a prepositional list onto a concession ("insofar as…", "including, among other things, …") until the sentence hits 45–60 words, and do not balance its members or break it up.
